content_html:
Buddhism, Neuroscience

In Buddhism, there is the idea that the totality of mind (and therefore memory) cannot be explained purely in terms of the physical brain.

Aspect Buddhist Perspective Neuroscientific Perspective
Nature of mind Mind (citta, vijñāna) is luminous and empty, not reducible to matter. It arises dependently and is part of a larger continuum beyond one lifetime (e.g., Yogācāra’s ālayavijñāna). Mind is an emergent property of neural activity; no evidence for existence independent of the physical brain.
Memory substrate Memories are karmic seeds (bīja) stored in the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), influencing future experiences and rebirths. Memories are stored in synaptic changes (LTP/LTD) and distributed engrams across hippocampus and cortex.
Continuity Consciousness and memory continue beyond death, conditioned by karma; not dependent solely on neurons. Continuity of memory is limited to the lifespan of the organism; after brain death, memories are irretrievably lost.
Explanation of recall Recollection is conditioned by karmic seeds ripening, sometimes described as accessing deeper strata of consciousness. Recall involves hippocampal pattern completion and cortical reinstatement of distributed neural traces.
Ultimate view Mind is fundamentally non-dual and not bound to physical processes; physical brain is just one condition among many. Brain is the sole known substrate of mind; all mental processes must be explained through physical architecture and dynamics.

Buddhism

  • Mind (citta/vijñāna) is not reducible to matter; consciousness (ālayavijñāna) holds karmic seeds. Continuity of consciousness across lifetimes.
  • Dependent arising; mind as process, not substance
  • Recollection via ripening of karmic imprints

Neuroscience

  • Mind as emergent from neural activity (physicalist)
  • Memory in synaptic/engram changes (LTP/LTD); Continuity limited to lifespan; no post-mortem memory
  • Mechanisms: hippocampal indexing, cortical reinstatement. Explains recall via network dynamics & plasticity

Overlap / Dialogue

  • Mind as process, impermanent and dependently arisen (Buddhism) ↔ dynamic, emergent neural activity (Neuroscience)
  • Shared practical interest in training attention/awareness and observing mind

Key Divergence

Buddhism allows for non-local, trans-lifetime continuity of mind; neuroscience restricts mind to the brain's physical architecture.
